PHASE 3 · ADVANCED HEALTH ASSESSMENT & CLINICAL DIAGNOSTICS

Week 54 — Lesson 78: Urgent Care & Emergency Assessment

FNP-level goal: Use first-contact triage to identify unstable physiology, activate the right level of care, begin safe immediate actions within scope, communicate a concise handoff, and avoid dangerous delays caused by premature diagnosis. This lesson is about clinical recognition and disposition—not substituting an app or a checklist for emergency protocols.

Learning Objectives

  • Distinguish routine outpatient, same-day urgent, emergency-department, and EMS-level presentations using physiology and trajectory.
  • Apply a first-pass ABCDE-style assessment: airway, breathing, circulation, disability/neurologic status, and exposure/context.
  • Recognize red-flag patterns for stroke/TIA, acute coronary syndrome, sepsis, respiratory failure, anaphylaxis, major bleeding, shock, acute abdomen, toxic/metabolic illness, and behavioral crisis.
  • Use diagnostic humility: stabilize and escalate before completing a low-yield outpatient workup when time-sensitive disease is possible.
  • Communicate an effective handoff with onset, vital signs, key findings, differential, treatment given, response, medications/allergies, and reason for escalation.
  • Document disposition, emergency precautions, and closed-loop follow-up safely.

Part 1 — Triage Is a Clinical Decision, Not a Scheduling Decision

The first FNP question is not “What is the diagnosis?” It is “Could this patient deteriorate or lose organ function if care is delayed?” Assess appearance, vital signs, mental status, pain, oxygenation/work of breathing, perfusion, bleeding, glucose when indicated, symptom onset/trajectory, and high-risk history. An apparently stable number cannot erase severe symptoms, a rapidly changing story, or a concerning examination.

Use the least restrictive setting that is safe, but do not use outpatient convenience, insurance, transportation, or fear of over-referral to delay care for an unstable patient. If immediate emergency care is needed, activate EMS or the local emergency pathway rather than sending the patient to drive themselves. Keep the patient observed and supported within clinic capability while help is arranged.

Part 2 — The First Pass: Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure

Airway: Can the patient speak? Is there stridor, swelling, drooling, vomiting/aspiration risk, or altered consciousness? Breathing: assess respiratory rate, work of breathing, oxygenation, lung sounds, cyanosis, fatigue, and ability to speak in full sentences. Circulation: assess pulse, blood pressure, skin temperature/color, capillary refill/perfusion, bleeding, chest symptoms, urine output where relevant, and signs of shock.

Disability: assess alertness, orientation, focal neurologic deficit, seizure, glucose when appropriate, severe headache, and behavior change. Exposure/context: examine the needed system while preserving dignity; ask about trauma, infection, medication/substance exposure, pregnancy possibility, anticoagulants, allergies, and relevant chronic disease. Repeat the first pass after any deterioration or intervention. Reassessment is part of treatment.

Part 3 — Shock and Sepsis: Perfusion May Fail Before the Diagnosis Is Obvious

Shock is inadequate tissue perfusion, not merely a low blood pressure reading. Concerning clues include altered mental status, weak pulse, tachycardia, cool/clammy or mottled skin, delayed capillary refill, oliguria, severe weakness, rising respiratory effort, and hypotension that may occur late. Consider hypovolemic, cardiogenic, distributive, obstructive, and other causes based on context, but do not delay emergency care while attempting to subtype shock in clinic.

Sepsis is the body’s extreme response to infection and is a life-threatening emergency. Infection plus confusion, shortness of breath, rapid heart rate/weak pulse, fever/shivering or feeling very cold, extreme pain, clammy skin, hypotension, or clinical deterioration requires immediate evaluation. Lung, urinary, skin, and gastrointestinal infections are common starting points, but any infection can progress. A normal initial temperature or a recent outpatient visit does not make sepsis impossible.

Part 4 — Chest Pain, Dyspnea, and Acute Coronary Syndrome

Chest pressure, tightness, pain, burning, shortness of breath, nausea, diaphoresis, palpitations, syncope, unexplained weakness, or pain in the arm, jaw, back, neck, or upper abdomen can represent acute coronary syndrome. Presentations vary by age, sex, diabetes, and comorbidity. Anxiety, reflux, or musculoskeletal tenderness cannot safely rule out ACS in a high-risk or concerning presentation.

Assess onset, exertional/rest relationship, associated symptoms, vital signs, ECG availability/competence, and immediate stability. Acute chest symptoms, concerning dyspnea, syncope, new arrhythmia, or suspected ACS require emergency/EMS evaluation. Do not delay transfer for serial office testing, a “GI cocktail,” or a routine laboratory draw. The FNP role is rapid recognition, safe first actions within protocol, and an accurate handoff.

Part 5 — Stroke and TIA: Transient Does Not Mean Benign

Think B.E. F.A.S.T.: sudden balance loss, vision change, facial asymmetry, arm weakness/numbness, speech/language difficulty, and time of onset. Sudden severe headache, confusion, trouble walking, new seizure, or focal deficit can also signal a neurologic emergency. Note last-known-well time, anticoagulant use, baseline function, glucose, and symptom course, but do not let a normal glucose or symptom improvement end the stroke pathway.

Transient symptoms can represent a TIA and require urgent evaluation. Call EMS for suspected acute stroke rather than having the patient drive. Record the time symptoms began or the last time the patient was known to be normal; this information affects emergency treatment decisions. A brief outpatient neurologic examination is not a substitute for an emergency stroke evaluation.

Part 6 — Respiratory Failure, Anaphylaxis, and Airway Threat

Respiratory emergencies include severe asthma/COPD exacerbation, pneumonia/sepsis, pulmonary embolism, pulmonary edema, upper-airway obstruction, anaphylaxis, aspiration, and metabolic acidosis with compensatory breathing. Red flags include severe work of breathing, cyanosis, silent/exhausted chest, inability to speak, altered consciousness, stridor, facial/oral swelling, hypotension, rapidly worsening symptoms, or hypoxemia in context.

Anaphylaxis is a potentially life-threatening systemic allergic reaction. Airway/breathing/circulation findings after a plausible exposure require immediate emergency treatment according to current protocol and EMS activation. Do not rely on antihistamine response or a mild initial appearance when airway symptoms, respiratory compromise, hypotension, or rapid progression are present. Monitor for change while awaiting higher-level care.

Part 7 — Bleeding, Acute Abdomen, and Time-Sensitive Pain

Major bleeding may present with visible blood, melena, hematemesis, hematuria with clots, heavy vaginal bleeding, trauma, or occult blood loss with pallor, syncope, tachycardia, hypotension, chest symptoms, or weakness. Ask about anticoagulants, liver disease, pregnancy possibility, trauma, and prior bleeding. Hemodynamic status and trajectory determine urgency; a reassuring first hemoglobin value or temporary symptom improvement does not always exclude significant acute loss.

Acute abdominal/pelvic pain needs a broad differential: ectopic pregnancy, appendicitis, bowel obstruction/ischemia, perforation, pancreatitis, cholecystitis, renal colic with infection, torsion, ruptured aneurysm, and other causes. Peritoneal signs, persistent vomiting, GI bleeding, hypotension, pregnancy with pain/bleeding, pulsatile mass/back pain, testicular pain, severe localized pain, or toxic appearance require emergency care rather than a routine outpatient imaging order.

Part 8 — Metabolic, Toxicologic, and Behavioral Emergencies

Consider glucose and metabolic derangement in confusion, weakness, seizure, diaphoresis, vomiting, dehydration, tachypnea, or unexplained behavior change. Suspected DKA/HHS, severe hypoglycemia, adrenal crisis, hyperkalemia, toxic ingestion, overdose, withdrawal, and heat illness require emergency pathways. Medication reconciliation, family/caregiver report, pill counts, and time line can be more useful than a narrow psychiatric label.

Behavioral emergency includes imminent risk of self-harm or harm to others, severe agitation with inability to maintain safety, delirium, severe intoxication/withdrawal, psychosis with unsafe behavior, or inability to meet basic needs. Use de-escalation, clinic safety policy, direct risk assessment, emergency/crisis pathways, and appropriate supervision. Do not leave a patient who cannot maintain safety alone to arrange ordinary outpatient follow-up.

Part 9 — High-Quality Handoff and Documentation

Use a structured handoff: patient identifiers and baseline; chief concern and onset/last-known-well; relevant history, medicines, allergies, pregnancy possibility; vital signs and trend; key examination findings; tests/treatments and response; working differential; and the exact reason for escalation. State what you are worried about, not merely the symptom: “possible sepsis with altered mental status and poor perfusion,” for example.

Document time of deterioration, EMS/ED communication, personnel contacted, treatments within scope, patient status at transfer, and any barriers. In a stable outpatient plan, document why emergency transfer was not indicated, return precautions, who owns pending results, follow-up timing, and how the patient will access the plan. Documentation supports continuity; it does not replace clinical judgment or emergency action.

Part 10 — Clinical Case: Confusion With Infection

A 72-year-old with dysuria now has fever, confusion, rapid breathing, weakness, and clammy skin. Blood pressure is lower than usual.

FNP reasoning: suspect sepsis with impaired perfusion. Activate emergency evaluation; do not treat this as uncomplicated cystitis or wait for a routine culture result.

Part 11 — Clinical Case: Transient Focal Symptoms

A 64-year-old had ten minutes of unilateral arm weakness and speech difficulty that resolved before the visit. They now feel “normal.”

FNP reasoning: transient focal symptoms can be TIA. Determine last-known-well time and arrange urgent emergency stroke evaluation; resolution does not make the presentation benign.

Part 12 — Clinical Case: Chest Pressure and Nausea

A 58-year-old with diabetes reports new central chest pressure, nausea, sweating, and shortness of breath while at rest.

FNP reasoning: this is an ACS pattern until evaluated. Activate EMS/emergency care and avoid delaying transfer for a routine outpatient diagnosis.

FNP Urgent-Care Assessment Framework

  1. First ask “Is this stable?” airway, breathing, circulation, mental status, perfusion, bleeding, glucose, pain, and trajectory.
  2. Recognize time-sensitive patterns: ACS, stroke/TIA, sepsis/shock, respiratory failure/anaphylaxis, major bleeding, acute abdomen, toxic/metabolic illness, and behavioral crisis.
  3. Escalate early: use EMS/emergency pathways when delay risks life, limb, brain, airway, or organ function.
  4. Do not overwork up in clinic: outpatient testing must never delay transfer for an unstable or high-risk presentation.
  5. Reassess continuously: repeat vitals and ABCDE assessment when condition or response changes.
  6. Communicate the concern: precise onset, vitals/trend, key findings, treatment, response, and high-risk differential.
  7. Close the loop: document transfer/handoff or an access-aware outpatient safety plan with exact emergency precautions.

High-Yield Summary

Triage: determine stability and risk of deterioration before choosing a diagnosis or appointment type.
Sepsis/shock: infection plus organ dysfunction/perfusion concern is an emergency pattern.
ACS: chest pressure, dyspnea, nausea, diaphoresis, syncope, or atypical symptoms in a high-risk patient need emergency evaluation.
Stroke/TIA: sudden focal symptoms—even if resolved—require urgent stroke pathway and last-known-well documentation.
Airway/breathing: stridor, swelling, cyanosis, exhaustion, severe work of breathing, or altered consciousness means immediate escalation.
Disposition: an outpatient order is not a safe substitute for emergency transfer when physiology or trajectory is concerning.
FNP standard: stabilize, escalate, reassess, hand off clearly, and document the reasoning.

Clinical safety note: This lesson is educational. Emergency assessment, medications, resuscitation, EMS activation, transfer, and disposition must follow current evidence, local protocols, scope requirements, and the individual patient’s presentation. In the United States, call 911 for an immediate medical emergency.
